title: The King Comes to Jerusalem
summary: Jesus rides into Jerusalem on a donkey and her colt, fulfilling Zechariah's picture of Zion's humble king, while the crowds hail him as the Son of David. He drives the traders out of the temple courts, heals the blind and the lame there, and defends the children's praise. The next morning he curses a barren fig tree, which withers at once, and teaches about faith and prayer. When the chief priests and elders challenge his authority, he answers with a question about John the Baptist and two parables, the two sons and the wicked tenants, which end with the rejected stone and the warning that the kingdom of God will be taken from them and given to a people who produce its fruit.
story:
Since Peter's confession in chapter 16 Jesus has been walking toward Jerusalem and telling his disciples that he will suffer, die, and rise there. Now he arrives, and the final week of his earthly life begins. Everything in Matthew 21 to 28 happens in or near the city within a few days, and chapters 21 to 25 form a single movement: Jesus enters as king, acts with authority in God's house, silences his questioners, pronounces woes on the scribes and Pharisees, and on the Mount of Olives speaks of the temple's fall and his coming.

This chapter is a public claim. Matthew's order is compact. The entry, the temple action, and the healings all happen on one day; the fig tree withers the next morning; and the confrontation with the temple authorities follows. The leaders' question, ‘By what authority?’, is the question the whole Gospel answers, and Jesus answers it by pointing to John the Baptist and then telling the first two of three parables of judgment (the wedding banquet follows in 22:1-14). The conflict that has been building since Galilee now moves to its center, the temple, and at the chapter's end the chief priests and Pharisees want to arrest him and hold back only for fear of the crowds. The plot sharpens from here to his arrest in chapter 26.
historical:
The setting is the days before Passover, in a year most scholars place at AD 30 or 33. Pilgrims from across the Jewish world filled Jerusalem, and many camped in villages like Bethphage and Bethany on the eastern slopes of the Mount of Olives, the ridge that rises across the Kidron Valley from the temple mount. Bethany lay about 3 kilometers from the city (John 11:18), and Jesus lodged there during the week (verse 17). The Mount of Olives carried prophetic weight: Zechariah 14:4 pictures the LORD's feet standing on it on the day he comes to judge and save, and Josephus tells of an Egyptian prophet in the 50s who led a crowd there promising that Jerusalem's walls would fall at his command (Antiquities 20.169-172). Judea was governed by a Roman prefect, Pontius Pilate (about AD 26 to 36), who lived at Caesarea but came up with troops at the festivals, since crowds celebrating Israel's liberation from Egypt could turn against Rome. Day-to-day authority in the temple belonged to the high priest, Joseph Caiaphas (about AD 18 to 36), and the chief priests, the leading priestly families, together with the elders, the heads of the city's great lay families (verse 23).

The temple was Herod the Great's rebuilding of the second temple, begun in the eighteenth year of his reign, about 20 or 19 BC (Josephus, Antiquities 15.380), and still being finished in Jesus' day. Herod doubled the platform to about 14 hectares (35 acres) and built along its southern side the Royal Stoa, a vast colonnaded hall (Antiquities 15.411-416), probably where much of the court's business took place. The outer court was open to Gentiles; a stone balustrade marked where foreigners had to stop, and one of its Greek warning inscriptions was found in 1871. The trade Jesus disrupted served real needs. Pilgrims needed unblemished animals and birds, and every Jewish man owed a yearly half-shekel for the temple (Exodus 30:13). The Mishnah says money changers set up tables in the temple on the twenty-fifth of Adar, about three weeks before Passover (m. Shekalim 1:3), and the temple's payments were fixed in the reliable silver of Tyre (m. Bekhorot 8:7). Doves were the offering of the poor (Leviticus 12:8), and the Mishnah recalls that Rabban Simeon ben Gamaliel forced down the price of a pair when it had risen to a gold denar (m. Keritot 1:7). The Babylonian Talmud preserves a lament over the high priestly houses of Boethus, Annas, Kathros, and Ishmael ben Phiabi, for their clubs and fists (b. Pesachim 57a), a later Jewish memory of a wealthy and violent priestly aristocracy. Jesus was not the only Jew to speak against the temple: Jeremiah had done so in its gate (Jeremiah 7, 26), and Josephus tells of another Jesus, son of Ananias, who from AD 62 cried woe against the city and the sanctuary, was flogged by the governor Albinus, and was released as a madman (Jewish War 6.300-309).

The blind and the lame who came to Jesus in the temple (verse 14) had long been kept at a distance from it. A saying attached to David's capture of Jerusalem declared that the blind and the lame would not enter the house (2 Samuel 5:8), the priests were forbidden to serve at the altar with such defects (Leviticus 21:18), and the Temple Scroll from Qumran forbids any blind man to enter the city of the sanctuary (11QTemple 45:12-14). Jesus heals them in the place from which they were barred.

The parable of the tenants reflects the agrarian economy of Galilee and Judea, where large estates owned by absentee landlords were leased to tenant farmers who paid a share of the crop through agents. The Zenon papyri, the archive of an agent of Apollonius, finance minister of the Egyptian king Ptolemy II, record in the third century BC an estate at Beth Anath in Galilee with some 80,000 vines, and Martin Hengel (1968) used them to show how realistic the parable's picture of an absentee owner and troublesome tenants was. John the Baptist, whose authority Jesus raises in verse 25, was widely honored as a prophet; Josephus says many Jews believed that Herod's defeat by the Nabatean king Aretas was God's punishment for John's execution (Antiquities 18.116-119). Matthew's first readers, on most datings, lived after Rome destroyed the temple in AD 70, and they would have heard the fig tree, the tenants, and the stone in the light of that catastrophe.
cultural:
Riding a donkey into the city was a deliberate sign. Pilgrims normally walked the last stretch into Jerusalem, and kings in Israel rode mules and donkeys on solemn occasions: David had Solomon ride his own mule to be anointed (1 Kings 1:33-40). Zechariah 9:9 pictures Zion's king coming humble and riding on a donkey, and the next verse says he will cut off the war horse and speak peace to the nations. The owner's willingness to release the animals when told ‘The Lord needs them’ recalls the right of kings and officials to requisition transport. Spreading cloaks on the road was a royal welcome (2 Kings 9:13, when Jehu was proclaimed king), and branches were carried at national celebrations: when Simon the Maccabee took the citadel of Jerusalem in 141 BC, the people entered with praise and palm branches (1 Maccabees 13:51), and branches were carried at the rededication of the temple (2 Maccabees 10:7).

The crowd's cries come from Psalm 118, the last of the Hallel psalms (113 to 118) sung at the great feasts. ‘Hosanna’ transliterates the Hebrew hoshi'ah na, ‘save, please’ (Psalm 118:25), which by Jesus' time had become a shout of praise as well as a plea. The Mishnah says worshipers shook their palm branches at those words during the Feast of Tabernacles (m. Sukkah 3:9), and that the priests circled the altar each day of that feast crying ‘Please, LORD, save us’ (m. Sukkah 4:5), so branches and hosannas belonged together in Jewish memory. ‘Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord’ was the priests' blessing on pilgrims arriving at the temple (Psalm 118:26). Matthew's crowd adds ‘to the Son of David’, making the welcome explicitly messianic, and when the city asks who this is, the crowds answer ‘Jesus, the prophet from Nazareth in Galilee’, a title of honor that falls short of what Matthew's readers know.

The children's praise (verse 15) shows how the acclamation spread. Children had no public voice, and the leaders' indignation at hearing them repeat the crowd's cry in the temple courts reflects both the danger of the words and the low standing of the speakers. Jesus answers with Psalm 8:2 in its Greek form, where God prepares praise from the mouths of infants.

Fig trees were among the chief trees of the land, and sitting under one's own vine and fig tree was a picture of peace (Micah 4:4). In the hill country near Jerusalem they put out leaves in spring, around Passover, together with small unripe knobs (Hebrew paggim) that were sometimes eaten; the first ripe figs came in early summer and the main crop in late summer. A tree in full leaf with nothing on it promised what it did not have. The prophets used the fig tree and its fruit as pictures of Israel before God (Jeremiah 8:13, Hosea 9:10, Micah 7:1), and the fruitless tree as a picture of judgment. ‘Moving mountains’ was a Jewish figure for doing what seems impossible; the Babylonian Talmud calls a brilliant teacher an ‘uprooter of mountains’ (b. Berakhot 64a).

To say something came ‘from heaven’ (verse 25) was a reverent way of saying ‘from God’. Tax collectors were local agents who bought the right to collect tolls and were despised as collaborators and cheats; prostitutes were among the most shamed people in the community. Both appear together as people who repented at John's preaching (verse 32; compare Luke 3:12, 7:29-30). The vineyard parable draws on Isaiah's song of the vineyard (Isaiah 5:1-7), where Israel is God's vineyard, planted, walled, and fitted with a tower and winepress, yet yielding only bad fruit. Jewish tradition read Isaiah's tower as the temple: the Aramaic Targum of Isaiah renders the tower as the sanctuary and the winepress as the altar, the Tosefta (t. Sukkah 3:15) makes the same identification, and a fragment from Qumran (4Q500), published by Joseph Baumgarten in 1989, links the vineyard's winepress with ‘the gate of the holy height’, the temple mount. Hearers who knew that tradition would hear in Jesus' parable a story about the temple and its keepers. The stone of Psalm 118:22, the ‘head of the corner’, was either a cornerstone binding two walls at the foundation or a capstone crowning the building; either way it was the stone the builders could not do without.
literary:
The chapter opens Matthew's long Jerusalem section (21 to 25) and is built as a sequence of symbolic acts followed by debate. The entry, the temple action, and the withered fig tree form a cluster of prophetic signs: the king arrives, inspects his house, and finds it fruitless. Matthew arranges Mark's material more tightly. In Mark, Jesus enters the temple, looks around, and leaves; the next day he curses the fig tree, clears the temple, and only on the third day do the disciples see the tree withered (Mark 11:11-21). In Matthew, the temple action follows the entry at once, and the tree withers ‘immediately’ (verse 19) before the disciples' eyes, so the sign and its lesson on faith stand together.

The entry is introduced by one of Matthew's fulfillment formulas, ‘This took place to fulfill what was spoken through the prophet’ (verse 4), which he uses about ten times. The quotation joins Isaiah 62:11 (‘Say to the Daughter of Zion’) with Zechariah 9:9, omits Zechariah's ‘righteous and having salvation’, and keeps ‘gentle’ (praus), the word Jesus used of himself in 11:29. Matthew alone mentions two animals, and in verse 7 Jesus sits ‘on them’, which may refer to the cloaks. When he enters, ‘the whole city was stirred’: the verb (seiō) is used for an earthquake, and Matthew uses it again when the earth shakes at the crucifixion (27:51) and the guards shake at the tomb (28:4). Jerusalem was troubled at his birth too (2:3).

The debate that follows (verses 23 to 27) has the form of a controversy story: a hostile question, a counter-question, and the questioners silenced. Matthew lets the reader overhear the leaders' private reasoning, and their answer, ‘We do not know’, is a refusal to decide. Then Jesus goes on the attack with the first two parables of a trilogy (21:28 to 22:14), each about Israel's leaders and God's messengers. Wesley Olmstead (Matthew's Trilogy of Parables, 2003) has shown how the three build on one another: the two sons concern John, the tenants concern the prophets and the Son, and the wedding banquet concerns the Son's feast and those later invited. In both parables of this chapter the leaders pronounce their own verdict, ‘The first’ (verse 31) and ‘He will bring those wretches to a wretched end’ (verse 41), whose Greek plays on the same word (kakous kakōs).

Matthew shapes the tenants parable in ways that point to the passion. The servants come in two groups rather than one by one; the son is thrown out of the vineyard and then killed (verse 39), where Mark has him killed and then thrown out (Mark 12:8), matching Jesus' death outside the city (compare Hebrews 13:12); and the verdict is spoken by the hearers. Matthew alone adds verse 43, one of his few uses of ‘the kingdom of God’ rather than ‘the kingdom of heaven’. The chapter is framed by the crowds: they acclaim Jesus as the prophet (verse 11) and at the end they still hold him to be a prophet, which is why the leaders fear to arrest him (verse 46).

outline.t: The humble king rides into Jerusalem
Jesus clears the temple courts and heals there
The fig tree withers: a sign and a lesson on faith
The parable of the two sons
The parable of the wicked tenants and the rejected stone

doctrines.note: Jesus publicly accepts the title Son of David and fulfills Zechariah's picture of Zion's king, but the king is gentle and comes on a donkey, not a war horse. In the tenants parable he places himself after the prophets as the owner's son and heir, and he applies Psalm 118's rejected stone to himself. His kingship is real and redefined at once: he rules as the one who will be rejected and killed.

Jesus acts as Lord of the temple, judging its trade by its calling as a house of prayer (Isaiah 56:7) and healing the blind and lame who had been kept from it. The withered fig tree signals that the institution in its present form will not stand, and the stone rejected by the builders becomes the cornerstone of a new house, which the New Testament identifies with the risen Christ and his people (1 Peter 2:4-7).

The fig tree and the tenants parable announce judgment on leaders who bear no fruit and reject God's messengers. The warning is aimed at those entrusted with God's vineyard, the religious insiders of the chapter, not at outsiders, and it asks every generation of leaders whether they treat God's people as their own possession.

The parable of the two sons defines obedience as a changed mind that leads to action. The verb for the first son's change (metamelomai) returns in verse 32: the leaders did not change their minds and believe even after seeing tax collectors and prostitutes do so. Repentance is measured by what a person does, not by what he promises.

Verse 43, ‘the kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a people who will produce its fruit’, has been read as God's rejection of Israel, as a transfer of leadership within Israel, and as the formation of a renewed people of Jews and Gentiles around Jesus. The chapter aims its warning at the chief priests and Pharisees (verse 45), while the crowds hold Jesus to be a prophet; how the verse bears on the Jewish people as a whole is a question Christians answer differently, and the church's history of reading it as a verdict on all Jews is a history it has had to repent of (see the hard question below).

words.note: Praus, gentle, humble, meek. It occurs only four times in the New Testament: in the Beatitudes (5:5), in Jesus' description of himself as ‘gentle and humble in heart’ (11:29), here in the Zechariah quotation (verse 5), and in 1 Peter 3:4. In the Greek Old Testament it renders Hebrew words for the humble poor who depend on God (Psalm 37:11). It describes strength that does not force itself, and it defines the kind of king who enters the city.

Hōsanna, a Greek spelling of the Hebrew hoshi'ah na, ‘save, please’, from Psalm 118:25. It occurs six times in the New Testament, three here (verses 9 and 15), twice in Mark 11:9-10, and once in John 12:13. By Jesus' day it had become a festival cry of praise. The Didache's table prayer already says ‘Hosanna to the God of David’ (Didache 10:6), and the word passed into the Sanctus of Christian worship. On the crowd's lips it is both a welcome and, without their knowing it, a prayer Jesus will answer by dying.

Lēstēs, robber, bandit, and in Josephus often a violent rebel. It occurs fifteen times in the New Testament, including the ‘robbers’ crucified with Jesus (27:38, 44) and Barabbas (John 18:40). In verse 13 it comes from Jeremiah 7:11, where the prophet accused Judah of treating the temple as a hideout, a den where robbers retreat after their crimes, trusting the building to protect them. The charge is not only about prices but about using worship as cover for injustice.

Sukē, fig tree. It occurs about sixteen times in the New Testament, four in this passage (verses 19 to 21) and again in the lesson of the fig tree about the signs of the end (24:32). In the prophets the fig tree and its fruit picture Israel's standing before God (Jeremiah 8:13, Hosea 9:10), and Luke tells a parable of a barren fig tree given one more year (Luke 13:6-9). Here the tree in leaf without fruit becomes an acted parable of judgment.

Exousia, authority, the right and power to act. It occurs about 102 times in the New Testament and is central to Matthew: Jesus teaches with authority (7:29), forgives sins with authority (9:6-8), gives his disciples authority (10:1), and after the resurrection claims all authority in heaven and on earth (28:18). The leaders' question in verse 23 goes to the heart of the book, and Jesus' refusal to answer it directly throws the question back on them.

Metamelomai, to change one's mind, to regret. It occurs six times in the New Testament: twice here (verses 29 and 32), of Judas's remorse (27:3), twice of Paul's regret over a letter (2 Corinthians 7:8), and in Hebrews 7:21, quoting Psalm 110:4 that God will not change his mind. It is not the usual word for repentance (metanoeō), and Judas shows that regret alone does not save, but here it describes a change of mind that issues in obedience.

Karpos, fruit. It occurs about sixty-six times in the New Testament and nineteen times in Matthew, from John's demand for fruit worthy of repentance (3:8) and the tree known by its fruit (7:16-20, 12:33) to this chapter, where the fig tree has none (verse 19) and the owner sends for his share of the fruit (verses 34 and 41). In verse 43 the kingdom goes to a people who produce ‘its fruits’, the fruit of the kingdom itself. Matthew measures faithfulness by fruit throughout.

Ethnos, nation, people. It occurs about 162 times in the New Testament, usually in the plural for ‘the Gentiles’ or ‘the nations’ (as in 28:19). In verse 43 it is singular, ‘a people’ (ethnei) producing fruit, and that choice is at the center of the debate over the verse. Some read it as the Gentile church replacing Israel; Anthony Saldarini (Matthew's Christian-Jewish Community, 1994) argued that ethnos could name a smaller group and that Matthew means a new leadership for Israel; others read it as a renewed people of Jews and Gentiles gathered around Jesus, like the ‘holy nation’ of Exodus 19:6 and 1 Peter 2:9.

christ:
This chapter shows Jesus as Israel's king, the Lord of the temple, and the Son sent last of all. The entry fulfills Zechariah 9:9, and Matthew says so explicitly. The king who comes is ‘gentle’, the same word Jesus used when he invited the weary to take his yoke (11:29), and Zechariah's next verse promises that this king will speak peace to the nations (Zechariah 9:10). The crowd hails him as Son of David, and in the temple the children repeat it, and when the leaders object, Jesus answers with Psalm 8, a psalm about praise offered to God. He accepts for himself the praise the psalm gives to the LORD.

In the temple he acts as the Lord of the house. Malachi had promised that the Lord whom Israel sought would suddenly come to his temple, and that his coming would refine it (Malachi 3:1-3); Matthew has already identified John as the messenger sent before him (11:10), which is why Jesus answers the question about his authority by pointing to John. If John was from heaven, the one John prepared for is the Lord of the temple. He heals the blind and the lame there, doing what the Messiah was expected to do (11:5), and in the next chapters he will announce that the temple itself will fall (24:1-2). At his trial the charge will be that he said he could destroy the temple and rebuild it in three days (26:61), and the temple curtain will tear when he dies (27:51).

In the parable of the tenants Jesus places himself after the prophets as the owner's son and heir, echoing the voice at his baptism and transfiguration, ‘This is My beloved Son’ (3:17, 17:5). He predicts that he will be seized, thrown out of the vineyard, and killed, as he will be crucified outside Jerusalem's walls. Then he applies Psalm 118:22-23 to himself: the stone rejected by the builders becomes the cornerstone, and this is the Lord's doing. The early church used the same psalm to speak of his death and resurrection (Acts 4:11, 1 Peter 2:7). The saying about the stone that breaks and crushes (verse 44) recalls Isaiah's stone of stumbling (Isaiah 8:14-15) and Daniel's stone cut without hands that becomes a kingdom (Daniel 2:34-35, 44-45), so that Jesus is both the foundation of God's new house and the kingdom that no power can stand against. The rejection that the leaders plan is the very means by which God makes Jesus the foundation of a people who produce the kingdom's fruit.
interpretation:
The entry into Jerusalem shaped Christian worship early. The Didache's eucharistic prayer (10:6) already cries ‘Hosanna to the God of David’, and the crowd's words entered the Sanctus and Benedictus of the Mass and of many Protestant communion orders. The pilgrim Egeria, visiting Jerusalem in the early 380s, described the Palm Sunday procession from the Mount of Olives into the city (Itinerary 31), and the Roman rite's procession of palms still sings the antiphon Hosanna filio David, from verse 9. In the Revised Common Lectionary, Year A, verses 1 to 11 are read at the Liturgy of the Palms. The historic Western lectionary also read the entry at the start of Advent: the 1662 Book of Common Prayer appoints Matthew 21:1-13 as the Gospel for the First Sunday in Advent, and the Lutheran one-year lectionary appoints verses 1 to 9, for which Johann Sebastian Bach wrote Nun komm, der Heiden Heiland (BWV 61, Weimar, 1714) and a second cantata of the same name (BWV 62, Leipzig, 1724). In art, Giotto (Scrovegni Chapel, Padua, about 1305) and Duccio (the Maestà for Siena Cathedral, 1308 to 1311) painted the entry with the donkey and its colt.

Matthew's two animals were read from early on. Justin Martyr (Dialogue with Trypho 53), writing in the mid-second century, linked them with Genesis 49:11 and took the harnessed donkey as a sign of the Jewish people under the law and the unharnessed colt as a sign of the Gentiles, both of whom would believe. The Babylonian Talmud (Sanhedrin 98a) records Rabbi Alexandri's reconciliation of Daniel 7:13 and Zechariah 9:9: if Israel is worthy, the Messiah will come with the clouds of heaven; if not, lowly and riding on a donkey.

The fig tree troubled readers from the start. John Chrysostom (Homily 67 on Matthew) explained that Jesus showed his power to punish on a tree rather than on people. Many patristic and medieval commentators read the tree as the synagogue, all leaves of observance and no fruit of faith, a reading that fed Christian contempt for Jews; modern scholars, following William Telford (The Barren Temple and the Withered Tree, 1980), mostly read it as an acted prophecy tied to the temple and its leaders. The temple action was read in the Reformation as a cleansing of abuses, as in Lucas Cranach's woodcuts for the Passional Christi und Antichristi (1521), and E. P. Sanders (Jesus and Judaism, 1985) argued instead that it symbolized the temple's coming destruction and renewal.

The parable of the tenants was read by the fathers as a summary of salvation history. Irenaeus (Against Heresies 4.36.1-2) traced the owner's servants through the prophets to the Son and the vineyard given to others, and Chrysostom (Homily 68 on Matthew) read the new tenants as the Gentiles. That reading, repeated for centuries, often slid into the claim that God had rejected the Jewish people and replaced them with the church, and it was given visual form in the paired statues of Ecclesia and a blindfolded Synagoga on medieval cathedrals such as Strasbourg (about 1230). After the Holocaust, the Second Vatican Council's declaration Nostra Aetate (1965, section 4) taught that the Jews should not be presented as rejected or accursed by God as if this followed from Scripture, and the Pontifical Biblical Commission's The Jewish People and Their Sacred Scriptures in the Christian Bible (2001) revisited Matthew's polemic in that light. R. Kendall Soulen (The God of Israel and Christian Theology, 1996) distinguished economic, punitive, and structural forms of supersessionism, giving a vocabulary for what the old readings assumed. Critical study asked whether Jesus told allegories at all; the Gospel of Thomas, found at Nag Hammadi in 1945, gives a shorter version followed by the rejected stone (sayings 65 and 66), and Klyne Snodgrass (The Parable of the Wicked Tenants, 1983; Stories with Intent, 2008) argued that the parable with its allegorical features goes back to Jesus. The Revised Common Lectionary reads the two sons (verses 23 to 32) and the tenants (verses 33 to 46) on consecutive autumn Sundays of Year A (Propers 21 and 22).
text:
English Bibles differ at several points in this chapter.

Verse 12: the KJV's ‘the temple of God’ follows later manuscripts; the earliest, including Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, read ‘the temple’. Verse 16 quotes Psalm 8:2 in the wording of the Greek Old Testament, ‘You have prepared praise’, where the Hebrew reads ‘You have established strength’; Matthew follows the Greek, and the verse is Psalm 8:3 in the Hebrew and Greek numbering. Psalm 118 is Psalm 117 in the Greek and Latin numbering.

Verses 28 to 31 are one of the most tangled places in the Gospel text. Manuscripts give three forms of the parable of the two sons. In the form printed by most modern Bibles, found in Codex Sinaiticus and many others, the first son refuses and then goes, the second agrees and does not go, and the leaders answer ‘the first’. In Codex Vaticanus and some other witnesses the order is reversed, the first son agreeing and not going, and the answer is ‘the latter’ (ho husteros); Westcott and Hort printed this form. In Codex Bezae and some Old Latin manuscripts the first son refuses and then goes, yet the leaders answer ‘the last’, the son who said yes and did nothing, which would make them answer perversely; the Latin Vulgate also reads ‘the last’ (novissimus). Editors have argued for each form, but all three agree on the point: doing the father's will is what counts.

Verse 44, ‘He who falls on this stone will be broken to pieces, but he on whom it falls will be crushed’, is missing from Codex Bezae, from minuscule 33, from several Old Latin manuscripts, and from the Sinaitic Syriac, and Origen does not cite it. It closely matches Luke 20:18, and some editors think it was added from there; others note that its position after verse 43 rather than after verse 42 is awkward for an addition. The Nestle-Aland text prints it in brackets, and the BSB, KJV, and most modern Bibles include it, some with a note.

teach.big: Jesus comes to Jerusalem as the gentle king and Lord of the temple, looks for fruit, and warns those entrusted with God's vineyard that rejecting the Son will cost them the kingdom, while the rejected stone becomes the foundation of God's new house.

outline.t: Jesus arranges his own entry to fulfill Scripture: Israel's king comes humble and peaceable, and the crowd welcomes him with words they only half understand.
The Lord of the temple judges worship that has become a hideout for injustice, and he opens the house to the blind, the lame, and the children whom others kept out.
The fruitless fig tree is an acted parable of judgment on leaves without fruit, and the disciples are called to a faith in God that prays boldly.
Jesus' authority comes from heaven, and those who refuse to decide about God's messenger cannot recognize the one he announced.
God's will is done by the son who changes his mind and obeys, not by the one who promises and does nothing; repentant outsiders are entering ahead of respectable insiders.
God is patient with those entrusted with his vineyard, sending servant after servant and finally his Son, and those who seize the vineyard for themselves condemn themselves.
The Son rejected by the builders becomes the cornerstone by God's own doing, and the kingdom belongs to a people who produce its fruit.

teach.pitfalls:
The most serious misuse of this chapter is to read the fig tree, the tenants, and verse 43 as God's verdict on the Jewish people. The chapter aims its warnings at the chief priests, elders, and Pharisees (verses 23 and 45), while the crowds regard Jesus as a prophet, and Jesus himself, his disciples, and Matthew's first readers were Jews. Teach the passage as a warning to all who hold religious responsibility, including church leaders, not as a charge against a people.

Other misreadings recur. The entry is sometimes taught as a picture of the fickle crowd who cheered on Sunday and cried ‘Crucify’ on Friday, but Matthew does not say they were the same people, and the crowds in Jerusalem protect Jesus from the leaders in this chapter. The temple action is sometimes used to justify anger or violence in general, or reduced to a lesson about church fundraising; it is a prophetic act by the Lord of the house. The fig tree is sometimes taught as a display of temper; it is an acted parable of the kind the prophets performed. Verses 21 and 22 have been taught as a promise that believers will receive anything they ask if they believe hard enough; the saying rests on faith in God, whose will Jesus himself submits to in Gethsemane (26:39), and it gives no warrant for treating faith as a technique. The parable of the two sons can be flattened into a lesson that intentions do not matter; its point is that repentance must issue in obedience and that God welcomes those who come late. Finally, the question of the two animals should be taught honestly rather than avoided or mocked (see the hard questions below).
teach.pastoral: This chapter may press on Jewish readers and on Christians who love them, since its verses were used for centuries to justify contempt and violence. Say plainly that the church has repudiated that reading and that Jesus' warnings are addressed to leaders, beginning with those who lead God's people now. It may also press on people hurt by religious institutions that treated worship as business or as cover for abuse; they need to hear that Jesus' answer to a corrupted temple was not cynicism but himself, and that he opened the house to those who had been kept out. The parable of the two sons offers hope to people who said no to God for years; the son who changed his mind did the father's will. People who have prayed with faith and not received what they asked should not hear verses 21 and 22 as an accusation; the one who spoke these words prayed in Gethsemane that the cup might pass and then accepted his Father's will.

hard.q: Did Matthew misunderstand Zechariah 9:9 and put Jesus on two animals at once?
hard.a:
The objection is one of the best known in Gospel criticism. Zechariah 9:9 describes the king riding ‘on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey’, a line of Hebrew poetry in which the second phrase restates the first, as Hebrew parallelism commonly does. Mark, Luke, and John have one animal. Matthew alone has two, a donkey and her colt, says the disciples put their cloaks ‘on them’, and says Jesus sat ‘on them’ (verse 7). Many critics conclude that Matthew misread the parallelism as describing two animals and then altered the story to match his proof text. John P. Meier and others have argued that no Jew familiar with Hebrew poetry would make the mistake, and some scholars have used the passage as evidence that the author of Matthew was a Gentile. Jewish critics of Christian proof-texting have cited it as an example of the Gospels shaping events to fit prophecies, and skeptics find the picture of a man riding two animals at once absurd.

There are several responses. Many commentators, among them R. T. France and W. D. Davies and Dale Allison, argue that Matthew, whose use of Scripture elsewhere is learned, understood parallelism perfectly well but followed a Jewish habit of making every word of Scripture count; Davies and Allison note that rabbinic interpretation often read poetic lines with deliberate literalness. David Instone-Brewer (Tyndale Bulletin, 2003) argued that first-century rabbinic exegesis did not treat parallel lines as mere repetition and that Matthew's reading would have seemed natural to Jewish interpreters of his day. Others argue that Matthew reports a genuine detail: an unbroken colt would go more calmly with its mother beside it, a point many commentators make, and Mark's note that no one had yet ridden the colt (Mark 11:2) fits that picture. On this view ‘He sat on them’ means on the cloaks, or on the animals in the loose sense that he rode one while the other went with it. Justin Martyr in the second century already knew both animals and read them symbolically (Dialogue with Trypho 53). Christians who hold a high view of Scripture differ on whether Matthew is reporting an additional historical detail or reading the prophecy in a Jewish interpretive mode; critical scholars differ on whether he misunderstood it. What is not in doubt is Matthew's point, shared by all four Gospels: Jesus entered Jerusalem as Zechariah's humble king, not on a war horse.

hard.q: Does verse 43 teach that God has taken the kingdom from the Jewish people and given it to the church?
hard.a:
The objection is grounded in the text and in its history. Verse 43, found only in Matthew, says that the kingdom of God will be taken away and given to ‘a people’ (ethnos) producing its fruit, and the parable it concludes ends with the owner destroying the tenants and giving the vineyard to others. The vineyard in Isaiah 5 is Israel. For centuries Christian preaching read the verse as God's rejection of the Jews: Irenaeus (Against Heresies 4.36) and Chrysostom (Homily 68 on Matthew) set out the parable as a history ending with the vineyard given to the Gentile church, and the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70 was presented as the owner's punishment. Jewish readers and many Christian scholars since the Holocaust have argued that such readings turned the Gospel into an engine of contempt; Rosemary Radford Ruether (Faith and Fratricide, 1974) traced Christian anti-Judaism to the church's christological reading of Israel's story, and R. Kendall Soulen (1996) named this kind of teaching punitive supersessionism, the claim that God has replaced Israel as punishment for rejecting Christ. On this view, whatever Jesus intended, Matthew's verse teaches replacement.

Responses begin with the verse's setting. Jesus says ‘taken away from you’ to the chief priests and elders (verse 23), and Matthew adds that the chief priests and Pharisees knew he was speaking about them (verse 45); the crowds, meanwhile, hold Jesus to be a prophet. The tenants are the vineyard's keepers, not the vineyard, and the vineyard is not destroyed, as it is in Isaiah 5, but given to other tenants. Anthony Saldarini (Matthew's Christian-Jewish Community, 1994) argued that ethnos can name a smaller group and that Matthew means a new leadership for Israel, the disciples who will sit on twelve thrones judging the twelve tribes (19:28). Wesley Olmstead (2003) argued instead that the ‘people’ is a renewed Israel into which the nations are now gathered, the fulfillment of the promise that Abraham would become a great nation. Others, including many traditional Protestant and Catholic commentators, read the ethnos as the church of Jews and Gentiles, while rejecting the conclusion that God has cast off the Jewish people, on the ground that Paul insists God's gifts and calling to Israel are irrevocable (Romans 11:1-2, 29). The Second Vatican Council (Nostra Aetate 4, 1965) and many Protestant bodies have repudiated the teaching that the Jews are rejected or accursed by God. Christians still differ on how the church and the Jewish people are related in God's purpose; what the verse itself indicts is leadership that treats God's vineyard as its own and refuses the Son, a warning that falls first on those who lead Christ's church.

observe: Which two passages of Scripture does Matthew combine in verse 5, and what does the crowd shout in verse 9?
What do the chief priests and elders say to one another before answering Jesus in verses 25 to 27?
In the parable of the tenants, what do the tenants do to the servants and to the son, and what verdict do the leaders pronounce in verse 41?
interpret: Why do you think Jesus chose to enter Jerusalem on a donkey, and what does Zechariah's picture of the king say about the kind of kingdom he brings?
How are the temple action and the withered fig tree related, and what do they say together about the temple and its leaders?
To whom does Jesus address verse 43, and how does the setting in verses 23 and 45 affect the way it should be read?
apply: Which son in verses 28 to 30 do you resemble more, the one who says no and then obeys, or the one who says yes and does nothing?
Jesus found leaves and no fruit. Where might religious activity in your life or church look healthy while producing little of what God is looking for?
If you hold any responsibility for others in your church, family, or work, where are you tempted to treat what God has entrusted to you as your own?
